title: The mobile visit for a developer-tool company
metaTitle: The mobile visit for a developer-tool site
excerpt: Engineers often open the link on a phone. The first screen still needs a real view of the tool and a way to try it. Do not let the desktop layout decide that crop.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The article is about a page that still has to work when the reader is away from that table, on a phone.
caption: The link is often opened away from the laptop on the table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a developer-tool page show on a phone?
faqs.answer: Show one sentence about the object the tool touches, a crop of the real output that stays readable, and a try control with a plain label. A slogan and a logo wall spend the only screen you are likely to get. Design that stack before you design the wide layout.

faqs.question: How should code samples behave on a small screen?
faqs.answer: Wrap them or cut them on purpose so a thumb is not stuck in sideways scroll. Show the important command and its result. Link to the full snippet in the docs for someone at a keyboard.

faqs.question: What makes the try button fail on a phone?
faqs.answer: A control that lands on a ten-field form, a silent copy with no confirmation, or a chat widget beside the target will lose the visit. Say what the tap does. If the install needs a laptop, say that, and do not pretend the phone is a workstation.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A developer-tool company mobile website is often the first review, even when the tool itself lives in a terminal or an editor. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing will open the link on a phone from a chat message. The first screen still has to show a real screen of the tool and a way to try the product. If those two survive the narrow width, the page can ask for a desktop later. If they do not, there is no later.

Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. Lock the narrow order first. The wide layout may place the snippet beside the sentence. It may not invent a hero that the phone would have to squash into an unreadable poster.

## The link arrives on a phone

Assume the visit starts in a chat or an email, on a phone, with a thumb and a short attention span. They are checking whether the link is worth a laptop. Your job is to settle that check. Show the mechanism. Show how to try it. Save the manifesto.

People leave weak pages quickly. Nielsen Norman Group's account of stay times puts the critical moment in the first 10 to 20 seconds. On a phone the screen holds less, so a slogan about empowering developers spends the entire moment and leaves no room for the tool. Put the artifact in that moment. Let the slogan go.

Open the live URL on a phone before you approve a desktop frame. Look at the first view only. Can you read the line the tool produced? Can you see the try action without scrolling past a newsletter and a logo bar? If either answer is no, the page is a desktop page with a shrink step, and the shrink step is the bug.

Type should be readable without pinch-zoom. If the sentence only works when they zoom, it is too long or too small. Shorten it until one breath holds it. Engineers will forgive plain type. They will not forgive a puzzle.

## The first screen, in one column

Stack the proof in an order that does not depend on side-by-side columns.

1. One sentence naming the object the tool touches.
2. A real screen, transcript, or snippet, cropped for the phone.
3. A way to try the product, with a label that names the mechanism.
4. The limit of the try, in one line, if a limit exists.

That is enough for the first view. A video, a logo wall, and a grid of principles can wait or leave. They are how the artifact gets pushed below the judgment.

The crop is the work. A full desktop screenshot reduced to phone width turns the mechanism into gray texture. Crop to the comment, the flag, or the three lines of the command and its result. You can use a different crop than the laptop uses. You cannot use a different, imaginary UI. The phone frame and the desktop frame should be the same truth at two sizes.

Code has to wrap or be cut on purpose. A horizontal scroll of a single clever line is how the try path gets missed, because the thumb is busy scrolling sideways. Break the example. Show the important flag. Link to the full snippet in docs for the person who has moved to a keyboard.

## The desktop does not get to go first

Designing the wide page until it looks finished, then collapsing columns, is how the try button ends up under a film and a quote. The phone stacks in source order. If the film is first in the document, the film is the product they meet. Change the order. The artifact leads. The film, if it earns a place, follows.

When you add a section, ask where it sits on the phone, not only where it looks balanced on a laptop. If it pushes the real screen down, it does not belong above the screen. Width is not a reason to introduce a new preface. The preface will follow them to the small device and cost more there.

Hover navigation is not a mobile plan. The jobs in the header, docs, pricing, changelog, try, have to appear in the phone menu as words. The try action should be visible even before the menu opens, beside the word mark. A skeptical reader will not explore a hamburger to discover whether they are allowed to run the tool.

Review both widths when you change a sentence. A line that breaks into an awkward stack on the phone should be rewritten, not squeezed. Rewriting is cheaper than a layout hack, and the shorter line usually helps the desktop too.

## A try path a thumb can finish

The action should be a real control with words. "Open the sandbox." "Copy install." Large enough to hit. Far enough from other links that a miss does not start a chat widget. If the control copies a command, say that it copied, in text, on the phone. A silent copy is invisible. They need the confirmation.

The destination has to work on the same phone or honestly send them to a laptop. A sandbox that runs in the browser can continue. An install that requires a shell should say "The command is copied. Run it on your machine." Do not pretend the phone is a workstation. Do not dump them into a sales form because the phone was inconvenient for you. The label and the result must match.

Keep the path short. Name, if you need an account at all. No ten-field profile. No required phone number. They can try and leave. A trial that demands a work biography will be abandoned with the tab, and the chat message that brought them will not get a second chance.

web.dev's write-up of Core Web Vitals is the performance bar for this view. A good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds, a good Interaction to Next Paint is within 200 milliseconds, and layout shift should stay at or below 0.1. A heavy web font that delays the snippet, a button that waits on a chat script, or a banner that pushes the try control down after load will fail the visit in a way this reader describes as "the site felt worse than the tool." Do not give them that description. Reserve space for the snippet. Let the page settle before they tap.

## Make the artifact readable in a pocket

Serve an image size fit for the phone. The laptop can have a larger file. The phone should not download a hero built for a conference slide. The ten-second judgment happens on ordinary connections, in offices and on trains.

Keep contrast high enough to read outdoors. A low-contrast transcript that looks refined on a calibrated monitor will vanish in daylight. The tool's actual colors should lead. If those colors fail on a phone, fix the crop or the surrounding page rather than washing the tool into a pastel it does not wear.

Do not put the snippet in a carousel. The second slide will not be seen, and the try button often sits in an unstable height while the carousel measures itself. Stack the one frame that matters. Offer the next frame lower, as a still, if the story needs it.

Docs pages need the same care. A docs layout with a three-column desktop design can become an unusable strip on a phone if the content column is an afterthought. The article column is the page. Sidebars can be drawers. The code sample is the content. Treat it as such.

## What waits below

Under the first view, add the limit, one hard fact, and a single proof. Where it runs. What it does not collect. A constraint and a decision with one small picture. Then repeat the try action for the person who scrolled to be convinced.

Pricing can be a link with the word pricing, or a stacked recommended plan if the shape is simple. Do not paste a wide comparison table and call it responsive. A table that requires sideways scrolling is a desktop document. Stack the plan they should start on. Put the other plans after, each with included and excluded in sentences if the table will not fit.

Skip the meetup photo, the manifesto, and the logo garden on this pass. They cost scroll. The phone makes the cost obvious. If a section does not help them try the tool or reject it for a clear reason, cut it on the phone and then cut it on the desktop so the site stays one story.

## Review it like a link from a chat

Send the URL to your own phone and open it one-handed. Do not review a resized browser and stop there. A narrow window is a clue. The device is the test.

Give it ten seconds. Look away. Say what the tool does and how to try it. Then actually try, as far as the phone allows. Copy the command. Open the sandbox. Count taps. If you are irritated, an engineer who does not care about your brand will leave faster.

Ask a colleague who did not build the page to do it from a real chat message, standing up. Watch for pinch-zoom and for the sentence "I'll open it on my laptop," said with doubt. Doubt means the phone page did not prove the tool. Change the crop or the order. Do not add a paragraph to compensate.

When the phone can show the screen and start the try, the next place people get lost is the path for humans. A contact page that behaves like an enterprise form will undo a clean first screen. Read [what that contact path should tell an engineer](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-developer-tool-company) before you add a required field.

If you want the narrow screen held to the same standard as the product UI, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the phone. The first view is the agenda.
